html:
CRISPR gene editing is a way to cut DNA at a chosen spot inside a living cell, published in 2012 by Jennifer Doudna of the University of California, Berkeley and Emmanuelle Charpentier. It made changing genes cheap, fast and precise enough for an ordinary lab.

The method borrows a defence system from bacteria. Bacteria keep snippets of virus DNA in repeated stretches of their genome called CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats), and use a protein, Cas9, to cut any matching virus that attacks again. Doudna and Charpentier showed that Cas9 can be steered by a short guide RNA to cut any sequence chosen. In 2013 Feng Zhang's group at the Broad Institute showed it working in human cells, which led to a long patent fight.

It is now used across biology, in crops and in medicine. In 2018 the Chinese scientist He Jiankui edited the genes of twin babies, an act condemned worldwide. Doudna and Charpentier won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020, and in 2023 a CRISPR treatment for sickle cell disease became the first to be approved. It builds on seventy years of work since the DNA double helix.
